blocks.text: Growing up in rural Pakistan, I was constantly aware that infectious diseases were not distant concepts—they were part of everyday life. I remember seeing adults who had been affected by smallpox, their faces marked permanently with dimples, signs of the illness. Those images stayed with me. They were a quiet but powerful reminder of what preventable diseases can do when protection is not available or accessible.

I also remember my own early vaccinations. I was immunized between the ages of eight and ten, and the process itself left a physical mark on me. The vaccine was administered in a way that left lasting scars on my arm, and even today, I can still see some of them. At the time, I did not fully understand the broader significance, but over the years I came to see those marks as a reminder of both vulnerability and protection—of what it means when public health efforts reach children consistently and effectively.

These early experiences shaped how I think about polio and other preventable diseases today. I have come to believe that addressing them is not only about medical intervention, but about ensuring fairness in access and opportunity. Every child should have the chance to be protected, regardless of where they are born or what resources their community has.

Over time, I also learned that health outcomes are closely tied to nutrition and overall well-being. A child’s ability to respond to vaccines and build immunity is not separate from their nutritional status. This reinforced my belief that health interventions must work together rather than in isolation.

Equally important is trust. Communities need confidence in both the intent and delivery of health programs. When services reflect local values, cultural expectations, and ethical considerations, people are more willing to participate and accept them. In my experience, this trust is often what determines whether public health efforts succeed or face setbacks.

Today, I see partnerships as necessary to moving closer to polio eradication. When organizations combine expertise, reach, and shared purpose, progress becomes not only possible but sustainable. Despite the challenges that remain, I remain optimistic. We are closer than ever to protecting children from diseases that once caused widespread suffering, and that progress is something worth continuing to pursue with urgency and care.

Sincerely,
Muhammad Munir Chaudry, PhD
President
